rationale: The 2025 bioRxiv original uses 18 Parkinson participants with minor hallucinations and 14 without, plus healthy controls. It relates resting functional connectivity and concurrent cognitive performance; the source reports no longitudinal food-linked visual episode comparison. The 2026 journal article is a later report of this sample.

The May 2026 medRxiv version starts with 178 participants from Newcastle and COMPASS-ND and analyzes 169 after quality control, including 83 with dementia with Lewy bodies. Its measured outcomes are imaging-derived cortical measures with molecular and spatial-map associations. It shares the analyzed sample with the journal article and gives no dried fig or food-timed measure.

The journal article uses 18 Parkinson participants with minor visual phenomena, 14 without hallucinations and 31 controls. Clinician assessments distinguish presence and passage phenomena, illusions or pareidolias, with overlap across categories. The paper describes cross-sectional functional connectivity and concurrent cognitive scores. The 2025 preprint describes the same Parkinson cohort.

The plasma-protein comparison enrolls 20 participants with dementia with Lewy bodies, 15 with mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer disease and 15 normal controls. No group protein result survived multiple-testing correction. Diagnostic and survival associations are distinct from measured food consumption or visual episode frequency.

The PDRisk account follows catecholaminergic imaging, CSF measures and incident diagnoses in people at risk for Lewy body disease, with clinical and postmortem observations for two cases who developed dementia with Lewy bodies. Biomarker trajectories and diagnosis provide no dried fig exposure contrast.

The retrospective cohort stratifies dementia with Lewy bodies by initial cognitive, motor or behavioral symptoms. Cognitive-onset patients progressed to dementia sooner in the observed cohort. Onset phenotype and later clinical domain observations provide no food-timed changes in visual episode count.

A clinical comparison evaluates virtual reality eye tracking for oculomotor dysfunction in Parkinson disease. Gaze and saccade features relate to Parkinson status and severity. Task-evoked eye behavior is a different outcome from spontaneous visual hallucination frequency.

In a preclinical Parkinson model, retinal measurements span synaptic transmission, inflammation, proteomics and structural changes. Visual hallucinations appear in the rationale for studying vision. The study measures retinal physiology and does not include a human visual endpoint or dried fig exposure.

This expert and trial synthesis covers initiation and maintenance of a subcutaneous medication and discusses prior hallucinations or psychosis as clinical context. The reviewed exposures concern drug administration, without a fig intervention or an original food-timed episode estimate.

The European perspective summarizes hallucinations, delusions and management of potential clinical and medication triggers. Its underlying evidence involves disease progression and drug or concurrent illness contexts. It offers no measured dried fig or dietary timing comparison.

Functional connectivity and specific cognitive domains are compared in 38 people with mild cognitive impairment with Lewy bodies and 24 healthy controls. The exposures are diagnostic group and task-independent network properties. The outcomes do not measure visual episodes after eating figs.

The full published proceedings contain independent hydrocephalus reports. One diagnostic member notes visual hallucinations and falls in a case with imaging-supported possible normal-pressure hydrocephalus. A separate shunt member tracks neuropsychiatric and functional measures. Neither measures a dried fig exposure, and the clinical cases are distinct.

The BioVRSea study pairs a virtual balance paradigm with EEG in Parkinson disease. Postural control and dynamic connectivity are recorded during the visuomotor task. This visual stimulation differs from clinical visual hallucinations and there is no food comparison.

The analysis codes how medicines are depicted in episodes of House MD and compares their portrayal with other fictional works. Its observations concern television content, without a clinical exposure or Parkinson symptom outcome.

Two case reports and a literature review track microscopic colitis during oral dopaminergic therapy and resolution following treatment changes. The observations concern bowel symptoms and drug routes. Dietary fig and visual episode frequency are outside the comparison.

An expert review synthesizes EEG responses to transcranial magnetic stimulation in multiple disorders. The Parkinson material concerns neurophysiology or stimulation measures. The review contains no food exposure contrast or recurrence estimate for visual episodes.

The diagnostic study analyzes DOPA decarboxylase in cerebrospinal fluid and other specimen types. Clinical grouping and biomarker performance address differential diagnosis in Lewy body disorders. No food exposure or visual event rate is measured.

Untreated, recently diagnosed Parkinson participants and controls undergo resting fMRI for network connectivity assessment. Follow-up helps confirm diagnosis. Connectivity measures have no linked dried fig consumption or clinical visual episode count.

The memory-clinic chart review compares patients by epileptiform activity on EEG. The measured outcome is electrical discharge status and its associated clinical characteristics. The design supplies no fig ingestion or Parkinson visual episode frequency.

The early Parkinson prediction analysis uses clinical measures and a limited series of repeated blood biomarkers to predict cognitive decline over five years. Cognition and model performance are distinct from a clinical food exposure and visual symptom assessment.

The autopsy-linked study uses onset data for clinical features from 949 patients who developed parkinsonism within three years of disease onset. The model predicts later neuropathological classification using clinical history. Occurrence or onset of symptoms provides no culinary exposure or episode-rate comparison.

The retrospective clinical series asks which patients assessed for idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus responded to shunting. Its exposure is surgery in another diagnostic group with motor and cognitive outcomes. Fig consumption and the frozen Parkinson symptom endpoint are absent.

The clinical and genetic case report describes a PUS3-associated leukoencephalopathy phenotype and longitudinal stability. It supplies a different population, with neither a dried fig comparison nor a measured Parkinson visual endpoint.

Sixty-two of 473 participants with a Parkinson diagnosis at follow-up were negative on a CSF alpha-synuclein assay. The study compares biomarker-defined phenotype and diagnostic change, with no dietary fig intake or episode response.

The imaging transcriptomics comparison uses data from 164 people with dementia with Lewy bodies and regional expression profiles. It models spatial relationships to brain atrophy. No meals or clinical visual episode rates are used as exposures or outcomes.

The study applies genome-scale models to infer patient-specific metabolite secretion patterns and summarize candidate Parkinson biomarkers. Predicted metabolites, including vitamin-related compounds, are distinct from a measured dietary source. It records no dried fig intake or visual episode frequency after food.

The review compares proximity ligation approaches to characterize alpha-synuclein oligomers. It cites a tissue association with visual hallucination presence in dementia with Lewy bodies. This is a cited neuropathological association without a culinary exposure or clinical recurrence measure.

Quantitative susceptibility MRI of 39 people with dementia with Lewy bodies and 30 controls compares tissue signal as an indirect marker of regional iron. Phenotype classification and image-derived measures do not establish dietary iron or fig exposure or visual event frequency.

The 359-person clinical series groups dementia with Lewy bodies participants by sleep profiles and relates them to disease onset characteristics. A psychiatric-onset group and sleep symptom prevalence do not supply a dried fig exposure or a rate of recurrent visual episodes.

This review describes pharmacological developments for Parkinson motor and nonmotor symptoms. Its interventions and limitations concern drug treatment and published drug trials, with no original dried fig and visual episode-frequency comparison.

The complete published congress supplement contains separate whole-diet protocols, a nutrition education pilot, dietary risk associations and medication or surgery psychosis analyses. No inspected member exposed a Parkinson cohort to dried figs and tracked visual episode frequency. The whole-diet, constipation and psychosis findings belong to distinct sets of participants.

The laboratory comparison tests homocysteine exposure and alpha-synuclein phosphorylation or aggregation in cell systems. It contains no measured link to fig consumption or actual clinical visual events.

The systematic review examines GABA-related magnetic resonance spectroscopy across 22 Parkinson studies. Regional neurochemical differences are distinct from the effect of any ingested food on clinical visual episodes.

The polysomnography-confirmed isolated REM sleep behavior disorder cohort includes 191 participants and compares features by CSF assay status. It describes clinical evolution and markers of prodromal disease without an ingredient intake or response in Parkinson visual symptoms.

The cross-sectional comparison tracks synuclein-related and nonmotor features in Parkinson disease and two progressive supranuclear palsy phenotypes. The comparison of symptom patterns and biomarker status does not measure timing after dried fig or Parkinson visual event rates.

The journal results analyze 83 people with dementia with Lewy bodies and 86 controls after quality control, as in the May preprint. Cortical shape and thickness, regional transcriptomic maps and connectivity are measured or compared. The design contains no food exposure or within-person visual episode-rate outcome.

The biomarker stewardship discussion describes how synuclein and neurofilament tests could inform diagnosis, classification and patient communication. These clinical uses do not supply food exposures or measured visual outcomes.

The 17-study systematic review covers longitudinal dementia with Lewy bodies biomarkers, including imaging markers of disease progression. Follow-up of biomarkers differs from testing a dietary exposure against visual episode frequency.
The research evaluates wearable motion data and classifiers for tremor, bradykinesia and dyskinesia. These motor measures and detection performance are unrelated to food-timed visual effects.

The NIMROD study relates inflammatory markers and PET measures to cognitive trajectories in dementia with Lewy bodies. Baseline inflammation and cognitive decline are measured without attributing them to dried figs, and the study does not count visual episodes after intake.

The retrospective genetic imaging analysis compares FDG PET metabolic signatures across genetic risk groups in dementia with Lewy bodies. Cerebral glucose uptake and model classification do not identify an individual food exposure or a visual outcome.

Of 50 consecutive advanced Parkinson patients who initiated subcutaneous treatment, two discontinued after visual hallucinations and both had prior psychosis. This implementation report counts discontinuations, without a controlled dietary exposure or recurrent visual episode frequencies.

The article draws on German clinicians' practical experience with subcutaneous levodopa and discusses protein and motor OFF timing as a possible clinical consideration. The clinical guidance and adverse-event discussion are separate. No individual dried fruit or food-timed visual outcome is tracked.

The review includes seven eligible studies. It treats delusions, delusional misidentification and visual hallucinations as related but distinct outcomes. The source includes no dried fig intervention and supplies no fig-attributed recurrent visual episode counts.

The review organizes animal Parkinson research by genetic and protein-model features and cites familial examples of visual symptoms. Experimental model readouts and a clinical genotype description provide no exposure–outcome comparison involving dried figs.

The study derives and internally validates a multivariable nomogram for future cognitive impairment in Parkinson disease. Predictors include clinical and neuropsychiatric measures. The predicted outcome is cognition with no food-timed hallucination comparison.
